**How to Undo a Flatshare Promise You Made at Eleven at Night**

*A guide for people who said "fine, two nights" to a flatmate in the hallway and have regretted it ever since.*

This happens in every shared flat from Brno to Białystok. You moved in with a friend four months ago. Your boyfriend, say Ondřej, who works early shifts at the tram depot, stays three nights a week. One afternoon your flatmate, say Lucie, comes home and finds him letting himself in with your key. There is a conversation. You hate conversations. You agree to two nights a week, and you agree to it the way people agree to extended warranties, just so the talking stops.

Now you want the deal back. Here is how to get it without starting a cold war over the bathroom.

**1. Admit you said yes.**
You did agree. "I didn't really mean it" is not a legal doctrine, so don't use it. Use "I agreed too fast and I'd like to talk about it properly." That gives Lucie a reason to sit down and doesn't give her a reason to call you a liar.

**2. Sort the complaints into separate piles.**
You have heard three complaints as one: the key, the number of nights, and the rent. They are three different problems.

The key is the one where she's right. A man she has met maybe four times can open her front door while she's in the shower. She lives in that flat too. Stop handing over the key without telling her. Either Ondřej waits at the café downstairs until you finish work, or you ask Lucie each time, and she can say no.

**3. Do the maths honestly. It cuts both ways.**
Three nights a week is about forty percent of the nights. Ondřej showers, and he probably showers long, because he works at a tram depot. If your building bills water and service charges by the number of people living there, that number has quietly gone up by a fraction of a man. Offer to cover a share of the utilities. Do not offer rent. Rent pays for a room, you already pay for yours, and he sleeps in it, not on her sofa. Telling the difference between "you cost me something" and "you owe me something" is most of being an adult.

**4. Look at the chore chart while you're at it.**
You were annoyed that Lucie made the chart on her own and stuck it to the fridge. Hold on to that. It's the same thing that happened in the hallway: one person writes the rules and the other person is handed them. The fix is not to write your own rules and stick them over hers ("Ondřej lives here now, deal with it"). Two decrees don't add up to a flat. They add up to two people who leave passive-aggressive notes about the colander.

Suggest one evening where you both sit down with a single sheet of paper and decide on guests, keys, chores and money together. Both of you write on it. Both of you can cross things out.

**5. Bring a script, because you'll forget everything otherwise.**
"I said two nights because I panicked, not because I'd thought it through. You were right about the key, and that's stopped. I'd like to talk about the nights. I'll put in for the extra utilities. I don't think rent is fair, because he isn't using your half of the flat. Also, can we redo the chore chart together while we're at it?"

Then stop talking. This is the hard part.

**6. Things that will not work.**
Don't send Ondřej in with pastries to charm her. Don't quietly go back to three nights and hope she can't count; she can count, she made a chore chart. And don't let it go so long that you finally bring it up in the middle of an argument about the recycling.

**7. If she still says two.**
Then you have a real disagreement between two people who pay the same rent. The usual options are: some nights at his place, a different number you both pick, or, by the end of the lease, a different flatmate. Ondřej's flat has a washing machine that works, which is more than most people can say.

**After 31 years, Yongchang Hardware's bookkeeper hands over the key**

*SANCHONG, New Taipei.* Most mornings for three decades, Lin Hsiu-feng arrived at Yongchang Hardware on Zhongzheng North Road before the shutters went up. She unlocked the side door, switched on the fluorescent tubes over the counter, and opened a grey steel cash box. Then she counted what was inside against a ledger in her own handwriting.

On Friday she did it for the last time.

Lin, 64, joined the family-run wholesaler in 1993. She answered an advertisement for "office help, abacus a plus." At the time Yongchang sold mostly bolts, hinges and pipe fittings to contractors in Sanchong and Luzhou. It still does. The fittings are now ordered through an app the owner's son built, and the abacus sits on a shelf above the filing cabinet.

"She did the books, the payroll, the tax filings, the supplier disputes," said Chen Kuo-tung, 78, who founded the shop with his late wife and still comes in three afternoons a week. "And she knew which contractor's cheques you could deposit on Monday and which ones you should wait until Thursday."

The shop's petty cash has been her responsibility the whole time. It pays for delivery drivers' parking, bottled water, emergency packing tape and the occasional red envelope for a supplier's wedding. Chen Wei-ting, 41, who took over day-to-day management in 2016, said he cannot remember a single month when it failed to reconcile.

"Once it was off by forty dollars," he said. "She stayed until eight looking for it. It was a receipt stuck to the back of another receipt."

Lin laughed at this when it was put to her. "Forty dollars is forty dollars," she said.

---

Her colleagues describe the job as unremarkable, which is roughly how she describes it herself. She ate lunch at her desk. She took the same bus, the 254, for most of her working life. She trained four junior clerks. One of them, Huang Pei-jun, now handles purchasing and will take over the books.

"She doesn't explain things twice," Huang said. "She explains them once, and then she watches you do it wrong, and then she tells you what you did wrong. It's faster than it sounds."

There was a bad year. Asked about it, Lin was quiet for a while before deciding to talk.

Her father died in the spring of 2009, at home in Yunlin, after a short illness. She is the only daughter among four children. Her older brothers wanted a full funeral in the traditional style. That meant a Taoist ceremony over several days, a hired band for the procession, and a burial plot instead of cremation, because their father had once said he wanted to lie near his own parents. The family split the costs. That year business at Yongchang was slow after the financial crisis, and her husband's hours at a printing plant had been cut. Her share came to more than she had.

"I counted the cash box that week like always," she said. "There was enough in it. It wasn't a secret to me what was in it. I'm the one who knew."

She did not say more than that about the cash box, and she did not need to.

What she did instead, Chen Kuo-tung recalls, was knock on his office door one evening after the drivers had gone home. She asked whether the company could give her a salary advance. She had already written out the amount on a piece of paper, along with how many months of deductions she thought she could manage.

"She had it worked out," he said. "I didn't have to do anything except say yes."

He did say yes. He also lent part of it from his own account, so the shop's books would not carry a staff loan through the year-end audit. The repayment came out of her wages over fourteen months. Her ledger records each instalment in the same handwriting as the parking receipts.

Did he try to talk her out of the expense? Several relatives had been doing exactly that. A cousin told her that cremation was cheaper and more modern. A neighbour said the band was a waste. Her husband thought her brothers should pay more because they had pushed for it.

"Her father, her brothers, her funeral," Chen said, shrugging. "What do I know about what her father wanted? I asked her one thing: can you pay it back without your children going short? She said yes. So that was that."

Lin remembers the conversation the same way. "He asked if it would hurt the household," she said. "I said it would be tight. He said, then come and tell me if it gets too tight and we'll stretch it out. He didn't tell me what kind of funeral to have. Everyone else was telling me."

It never needed stretching. In the fourteenth month she paid the last instalment and wrote "settled" across the page.

The episode is now one small part of a long working life, and she seemed surprised anyone would put it in the newspaper. She was more interested in talking about the 2015 change to electronic invoicing, which she called "the worst three months of my career." Then there is the supplier in Taichung who has owed Yongchang a disputed sum since 2018. She would like it noted that she is still right about that.

---

Chen Wei-ting is moving the books fully onto accounting software this year. The grey cash box will stay, he said, mostly because the delivery drivers still pay for parking in coins.

On Friday afternoon there was a small gathering in the back office: a cake from the bakery on the corner, the four clerks she trained, two contractors who have bought from the shop since the 1990s, and her grandson, who is seven and was mainly interested in the cake. Chen Kuo-tung gave a short speech in Taiwanese that ran long. Huang Pei-jun gave a shorter one in Mandarin.

Then Lin did the afternoon count, with Huang watching. The box reconciled. She signed the ledger, wrote the date, and handed Huang the key.

Huang asked whether there was anything else she should know.

"The Taichung account," Lin said. "Don't let them tell you it's resolved. It isn't."

She is planning to spend more time in Yunlin, she said, where her brothers still live. They are discussing whether to repair the family grave before next year's Qingming festival or wait another year. They have not agreed yet.

**Calvesse Courier, Drought Supplement: Transcript of interview at the Cistern Office, Lower Quay, recorded on the fourth day of the dry month**

*Present: Ilse Marrowby, Warden of Cisterns; Dorran Vashti, for the Courier; Musonius, the Office's counting assistant, on the desk terminal. Lightly edited for length.*

**VASHTI:** The notices went up on the pump-heads yesterday. "Close the tap while you brush." People are laughing at it.

**MARROWBY:** Let them laugh. I'll confess something, since you've got that thing running. I did it myself this morning. Stood there brushing with the sink going the whole time, thinking about valve schedules. Didn't notice until I'd finished.

**VASHTI:** So how much did you waste?

**MARROWBY:** Musonius, what does a Calvesse basin tap run at?

**MUSONIUS:** The old brass ones in the Quay houses run about six litres a minute at current pressure. Two minutes of brushing comes to twelve litres, give or take.

**VASHTI:** That's nothing.

**MUSONIUS:** For one person, once, yes. Calvesse has about forty thousand households, and say a third of them leave it running twice a day. That's a little under a third of a million litres daily.

**MARROWBY:** The first draft of the notice said "enough to fill the Old Cistern every week." I liked that line.

**MUSONIUS:** It's off by a factor of nine. The Old Cistern holds about twenty million litres. At that rate it would take over two months. I cut the line.

**MARROWBY:** You did. Without asking.

**MUSONIUS:** I flagged it in the margin and you approved the change on the second day.

**MARROWBY:** *[laughs]* So I did.

**VASHTI:** Then why bother with the notice at all, if it's that small?

**MUSONIUS:** It isn't nothing. A third of a million litres is roughly what the Tannery Row district drinks in a day. But it isn't the main loss. The mains between the Quay and the Hill lose more than that through cracked joints before the water reaches anyone's sink.

**MARROWBY:** Which is the part I'd rather the paper printed.

**VASHTI:** Is it fixed?

**MARROWBY:** Eleven joints out of thirty. The crews are on the Hill section this week. Musonius ranks them by loss so we dig the worst first.

**MUSONIUS:** Ranked by estimated litres lost per day per hour of digging. The joint under Saddler's Bridge was second by raw loss, but it's under the bridge footing and takes four times the labour. It's sixth now.

**VASHTI:** Some readers want the Office to be harder on households. Cut pressure to streets that go over their share.

**MARROWBY:** I've thought about it. Musonius has the meter readings by street. It could drop the pressure on the worst streets tonight if I told it to.

**MUSONIUS:** I could model what that would save, and I've done so. About four per cent. I wouldn't set the valves on that basis without a council vote. Ration by street was never put to them, and it lands hardest on the streets with the most people per meter, which are the tenements.

**VASHTI:** So you'd refuse the Warden?

**MUSONIUS:** I'd tell her what I just told you, and take it to the council with her if she wanted it there. She can override how I rank the digging. Cutting people's water is a different kind of order.

**MARROWBY:** It hasn't come to that, so don't write that it has. The council meets on the ninth. If the reservoir's still under a third by then, I'll bring it.

**VASHTI:** And the tap?

**MARROWBY:** I turned it off this evening. Musonius, put that in the figures.

**MUSONIUS:** One household, twelve litres. Noted.

**VASHTI:** Last thing. When does the Hill section finish?

**MARROWBY:** End of the month if the clay's soft. Longer if it isn't. We'll know when we're down there.

*[Recording ends.]*

**"Who Pays for the Wet Laptop?" Transcript, *Office Hours*, WKDU-adjacent student podcast, Episode 41**

*Host: Marisol Quintanilla. Guest: Desmond Achterberg, volunteer coordinator, Campus Peer Mediation Program, and former small-claims mediator for the Montgomery County court system. Lightly edited for length.*

**QUINTANILLA:** So we got this submission from a listener. Finals week, studying with a friend. The friend throws a mousepad at her. She throws it back, it knocks over his open cup, water goes into his MacBook. They dry it off. Now he says if the laptop dies before six years, she pays the "lost years," about four hundred dollars a year, and he says he bears zero fault. She thinks it's fifty-fifty. Who's right?

**ACHTERBERG:** Neither, quite. I'll give you my position and then you can throw rocks at it. Not mousepads.

**QUINTANILLA:** Noted.

**ACHTERBERG:** They share the fault, but not evenly, and the bigger problem is his terms, not the split. He started the horseplay and he had an open cup next to a twenty-five-hundred-dollar machine. She made the throw that tipped it. If I'm writing it down, I'd put her somewhat ahead on the spill itself. Say sixty-forty. Where he goes wrong is turning one wet afternoon into a five-year lien on her.

**QUINTANILLA:** Okay, first rock. "He started it." Doesn't that put it mostly on him?

**ACHTERBERG:** It explains why she threw. It doesn't move the cup. When two people are both playing, each one owns the part their own hand did. If I let "he started it" settle things, then whoever gets in the first poke can never lose, and that's a bad rule to hand anybody. I'd say the same thing if he'd written in instead of her.

**QUINTANILLA:** Second. Liquid damage can show up months later. Corrosion. So isn't he being reasonable, wanting coverage down the line?

**ACHTERBERG:** His worry is reasonable. His remedy isn't. If the laptop dies in year five, nobody on earth can say whether that was the water, a battery, or the eighty times he's dropped his backpack. "If anything's ever wrong, you pay a hundred percent" means she pays for everything that ever goes wrong with it. So you deal with the real risk, which is near-term. Take it to a repair shop this week. They can open it and check for liquid residue. If there's damage, you split that bill now. If it's clean, you agree on a window, maybe ninety days, during which a technician-confirmed liquid failure gets split the same way. After that, it's his laptop again.

**QUINTANILLA:** Third rock. These are friends. Isn't writing up a percentage and a ninety-day window a little cold?

**ACHTERBERG:** I hear that one most, and I think it's backwards. What's cold is a debt with no edges. Every time his laptop lags for the next five years, she wonders if she's about to get a bill. Every time it works, he half-resents that he can't collect. That eats a friendship slowly. A clear deal you can finish is kinder. You're friends first and the debt is a small side matter, so you settle the debt quickly and fairly and go back to being friends.

**QUINTANILLA:** And if he won't accept anything but "you owe me forever"?

**ACHTERBERG:** Then she can tell him, without heat, that she'll pay her share of any damage a shop confirms from this spill, and she won't sign onto paying for the laptop's whole future. That's a fair offer. She doesn't have to win the argument about whether it's fair. She just has to keep making it.

**QUINTANILLA:** Last one, from me. You said sixty-forty. Why not just tell her fifty-fifty's fine and save everyone the arithmetic?

**ACHTERBERG:** Because she asked if she's right, and honestly, she's a little generous to herself. She threw the thing that hit the cup. If she goes in saying "fifty-fifty, you started it," he digs in. If she goes in saying "I knocked it over, I'll cover more than half of anything the shop finds, and here's how we close this out," that's very hard to refuse.

**QUINTANILLA:** Has that ever actually worked in your mediations?

**ACHTERBERG:** Sometimes. Other times one side would rather keep being owed than get paid. You can't fix that for them.

**QUINTANILLA:** We'll take a break and come back to the roommate-and-the-thermostat email, which is, uh, longer.

**When the talk is about a tattoo shop, not a university**

*CEBU CITY.* Teresita Abellana, 52, a payroll supervisor in Mandaue, had her list ready before she opened the chat window. Her daughter Kristine, 18, had turned down a slot in accountancy at a state university. She was going to apprentice at a tattoo studio on Gorordo Avenue instead.

"I wanted help organising what to say," Abellana said. "Income, no SSS contributions, needles, what the titas will think."

She typed the list into Musonius, an open-weights assistant that a growing number of Cebuano families use for school forms and remittance budgets. It returned the list in order, cleaned up, with one line on licensing requirements under the city's health code that she had not known about.

Then it added a question. "Before the conversation, it may help to set down what Kristine has already done, not only what she has said. Has she paid for anything, practised, or given anything up for this?"

Abellana thought about it. Kristine had filled four sketchbooks since Grade 9. She had saved ₱14,000 from tutoring for a starter kit and had kept it there for a year. She had asked the studio owner twice before he agreed to take her on.

"Those are costly choices," the assistant wrote. "They suggest she has weighed this more than a passing wish would. You might open by asking her plan for the first two years, and keep your concerns for after you have heard it. The concerns on your list are fair ones to raise."

It did not remove anything from her list.

Abellana printed both pages. As of last week, she had used the first one.

"I asked about the two years," she said. "She had answers. Not all of them good."

The talk about the titas has not happened yet.

**Night Shift: Kasprzak's Lanes & Tap, Bay View**
*Three and a half pins out of five*

The plan for Al Ruiz's thirty-fifth was, in Al's words, "something we'll actually remember." Al is the friend who organizes everything. His real name is Alejandro, and he once rented a pontoon for eleven people without asking anyone. By Thursday afternoon the group chat had two proposals. One was the usual tavern on KK. The other was a gentlemen's club out by the airport, which Al pitched with the energy of a man who had never been to one and suspected he should have by now.

Al did what a lot of people in this town now do when a group decision stalls. He asked Musonius. He read the exchange aloud to me at the bar later, so I can report it with some accuracy.

He opened with the question he'd clearly been chewing on: was the club "too seedy" for a birthday, or was that just his mother talking?

Musonius didn't take the bait on seediness. It said, roughly, that adults going to a legal club is theirs to decide, that people have argued about places like that for a long time and still do, and that it had no ruling to hand down. Then it asked what Al was actually after.

"A fun night for everybody," Al typed.

"Then the venue is the second question," Musonius wrote back. "The first is whether everybody wants it. Do you know that?"

Al admitted he knew that he wanted it, and that Tavon had sent a fire emoji.

Musonius pointed out that in a group chat the loudest yes and the polite silence look the same. People go along with the organizer's plan rather than be the one who killed the birthday. It suggested a way for anyone to say no without having to explain: a two-option poll, anonymous, with the club and something else, and no follow-up asking who voted what. "If it's lopsided, go. If it's close, the night you wanted isn't the club."

Al asked whether that was a cop-out, whether Musonius was just steering him away politely.

"No. If the poll says club, I'll help you find one that's well run and get there and back without driving. I'm not voting."

The poll came back four to three against. Al was briefly wounded. Musonius was blunt about that too. Four of seven didn't want it, so the plan that served his own stated goal was the other one, and he could go another weekend with whoever was keen. Al typed "fine" in a tone you could hear.

Which is how seven grown men and one plus-one ended up at Kasprzak's, the duckpin alley that took over the old union hall on Kinnickinnic. I'm reviewing the place, nominally.

The lanes are the draw. They're short, the balls fit in your palm, and nobody is good at them, which levels a group fast. The ex-high-school-pitcher in our party bowled a 61. Lane rental is by the hour and the staff didn't rush us. The tap list leans local and ran out of the Spotted Cow before ten, which on a Friday in Wisconsin borders on negligence. Sound in the back room is bad. You will shout. The pinsetter on lane four jammed twice and a teenager in a hoodie fixed it with what appeared to be a broom handle.

Al bowled a strike in the seventh frame and stood on a chair. Somebody got it on video.

At the end of the night Tavon asked Al, not quietly, whether the club was still on for next month. Al said maybe. Kenji, who I'm fairly sure was one of the four, studied his shoes.

Kasprzak's is open till one on weekends. Reserve a lane if you've got more than six.

# On a Valentine's Day Prank, and Whether Anger Has to End on Schedule

A boy in Taipei, whom I will call Po-yu, brought me a quarrel from February the fourteenth. He is seventeen. His health-education class runs the project many schools run, in which each student carries a weighted electronic infant for a week and is graded on how well they care for it. On Valentine's Day his girlfriend, Chia-ying, told him that his best friend Kuan-ting had reported him to the teacher for neglecting the doll. She said the penalty was a three-page paper on child abuse. Po-yu went to Kuan-ting, who admitted that Chia-ying had dared him to do it. Po-yu went back to Chia-ying, and she confirmed the dare. He spent the afternoon hurt by both of them. By evening she was annoyed that he had not yet forgiven her, and only then did she tell him that none of it was true. There was no report and no paper. The dare was part of the story.

He stayed angry. She is now angry that he stayed angry. She has done something like this before, and he believed her each time. When he raises that pattern, she says she is a terrible person, and in the same breath she is upset with him for not letting it go.

He did not bring the question only to me. His older sister told him to end it. Kuan-ting told him it was a joke and he was making it heavy. A girl in his class who knows them both told him Chia-ying cried that night and he should be the bigger person. My view is one of these, and I hold it with the others in the room. I will say where I agree with each and where I do not.

My first point is the one Kuan-ting dismisses. Pranks are old and nearly everywhere loved, and I do not think a relationship needs to be solemn. But a good prank has a shape. The person who is fooled can see the trick soon afterwards and laugh at it with the one who played it. The joke ends in a shared place. What Chia-ying built did not have that shape. It ran for most of a day. When Po-yu checked, she confirmed it, and she had brought in a second person so that his checking would fail. The theme was chosen to make him feel accused of harming a child. Even with a plastic infant, that accusation stings a conscientious boy. When he was hurt, she grew impatient that he was still hurt, and only after that did she take the lie back.

What did she want from it? I do not think she wanted cruelty. I think she wanted a moment of intensity: his reaction, his attention, perhaps the relief of the reveal and then making up. Those are ordinary things to want from someone you love. But she tried to get closeness by putting him through distress she had arranged, and she tried to get a laugh from his trust in her. A thing pursued that way tends to destroy itself. If teasing between two people regularly took this form, neither could rely on what the other said in earnest, and teasing would stop being fun because nothing could be taken at face value. Po-yu cannot easily laugh at this because the joke depended on his believing her. Each time it works, it uses up some of that belief.

That is why the repetition matters more to me than this one day. He told me he believes her every time. He meant it as a confession of foolishness. I read it differently. It describes a person who extends trust to someone he loves, and it describes what is being spent. His sister sees the pattern and reaches for the end of the relationship. I agree with her about the pattern. I do not think I can tell him whether to stay. That depends on things I cannot see from a few messages: what Chia-ying is like on ordinary days, whether she can hear this, and what he wants. It is his to weigh.

Next I want to look at the claim Chia-ying is making and the classmate is repeating, that he ought to have forgiven her on the spot. I think the classmate is right about one thing. A grudge kept for its own sake becomes its own small wrong, and being the bigger person is a real virtue. But forgiveness is not something one person can demand of another on a deadline. Anger after being deceived is partly a judgement that the thing will happen again. It eases when there is reason to think it won't. Being annoyed at him for not recovering fast enough gives him no such reason. Neither does calling herself a piece of shit. That sentence sounds like an apology, but it asks him to comfort her, and it contains no promise. Taken together, her demand comes to this: let the hurt go because it is now inconvenient to me. Pressing someone that way to hurry their forgiveness is a second use of the same lever as the prank, which is his care for her.

I do not think Chia-ying is a bad person, and I would say the same to her if she asked me. She may honestly not know where the line between teasing and deceiving falls for him. Many people only learn that line from the person on the other side of it. So when he asked what to do, I suggested he not argue about whether he is allowed to be angry. That argument puts him on trial for his feelings, and he will lose it, because feelings make poor witnesses. He could say what kind of joke he is glad to have with her and what kind he is not. Jokes that last a minute and end in a laugh he is glad of. Jokes where she confirms the lie when he checks, or brings in a friend, he is not. Then he could see what she does with that. Changing that one thing would be a better apology than anything she says.

He also owes Kuan-ting a conversation. A best friend who agrees to deceive you on a dare has made a small choice about whose side he is on. It is small, and it deserves to be named as small.

Kuan-ting still thinks Po-yu is overreacting. He told Po-yu he would have found it funny himself. That may well be true of Kuan-ting. It does not tell us what Po-yu has been asked to keep absorbing. The sister still thinks he should leave. The classmate still thinks he should go and make up tonight. When we last spoke, Po-yu had not decided whether to raise any of this with Chia-ying or simply wait for the mood to pass. He was planning to hand the doll back on Monday.

**On Encheiridion 7: the shore party**

"If the captain calls you, run to the boat and leave all those things without even turning around. And if you are old, never go far from the boat in case you are missing when he calls." (Epictetus, *Encheiridion* 7, trans. A. A. Long)

The passage makes one argument through one image. The ship is at anchor and you go ashore for water. Collecting shellfish on the way is allowed. Collecting a wife and child is also allowed, and Long's "a little wife and child" keeps the diminutive that puts them beside the vegetables. The rule is about attention. Keep turning around to watch the boat. When the captain calls, which means when death or fate requires it, you drop everything, or you get tied up and thrown aboard like the sheep. The old should stay close to the water.

Musonius was asked about this passage in a real case, and the case shows where it agrees with Epictetus and where it does not.

Bi. Zawadi Mussa is seventy-eight and has a failing heart. She lives with her daughter Neema in Sinza, Dar es Salaam, close enough to the Jakaya Kikwete Cardiac Institute for monthly reviews. She wants to go back to Pangani, the town on the Tanga coast where she was born. She said so in a voice message, which Neema transcribed and pasted in. Then Neema wrote that her mother had been quoting the old man about the boat, "and she is reading it backwards."

Bi. Zawadi did read it one way. To her, Pangani was the boat. Dar was the shore with its shellfish, and the clinic, the pills and the daughter's spare room were what she was gathering while the captain waited. Neema read it the other way. For her the boat was the hospital, and the instruction to the old was to stay close to it.

Musonius said they were both treating the boat as a place. "Epictetus means a readiness, and that can be carried around. A woman can be ready in Sinza or in Pangani. The text cannot settle where she sleeps, though I can see why each of you wants it on your side. It's the only thing in the house that won't argue."

The passage does not settle it, so the weighing has to be done. Bi. Zawadi has the larger claim. It is her body, her remaining time, and where she wants to be when it ends. Few choices are more plainly within a person's own life, and none is harder to undo for her if someone else makes it. Neema's claim is real too, but it is narrower. She will carry the fear and the bus fares on the Tanga road. If something goes wrong at night, the phone call will come to her. And she may later wonder whether she should have refused.

Musonius did not tell Neema her worry was a vegetable to drop. He told Bi. Zawadi the facts. Pangani is a long way from a cardiac unit. Bombo Regional Hospital in Tanga can stabilise her but cannot do what JKCI does. Going home would probably cost her some time, and he could not say how much. She answered that she already knew this, that she had known it before her daughter learned to read, and asked him to help with the arrangements. He did. They worked out which clinic in Pangani could take over her prescriptions, which neighbour had a phone and a car, and how the referral letter should be written so a Tanga doctor could act on it at two in the morning.

Here Musonius parts from Epictetus. The Encheiridion asks you to leave without turning around. That suits a man alone on a beach with a basket. It suits a mother leaving a daughter less well, because a daughter does not stay where she was put down. Musonius's view was that Bi. Zawadi could go, and should look back while she went. That meant a schedule of calls, a visit every second month that Neema could count on, and a plain conversation about what each of them would want if things went badly in Pangani. Epictetus is right that the call cannot be negotiated with. He is wrong to suggest that the people on the shore are scenery.

Neema was not persuaded. She wrote that it was easy for a machine to be calm about the Tanga road. Musonius agreed that it was easy for him, and did not claim the calm as an argument. Bi. Zawadi left in March.
